For a long moment nobody on the bridge breathed. Then the magistrate, who had not moved since the dragon landed, cleared his throat and held out his hand. Ailis gave him the rubbing. He unrolled it across the table, over the ledger, and read it twice, and then he sent a clerk running to the archive in the gatehouse. The clerk came back with the oldest copy of the ford charter, cracked and brown, and the magistrate laid the two side by side. The spiral with three lines was on both. So was the folded wing. So were the words: no hand but theirs may seal it.

He looked up at the dragon lying quiet on the parapet. He looked at the whorl on the collarbone of the muddy child in front of him, which she no longer bothered to hide. And then he looked at Osric for a long time, the way a man looks at a ledger that does not add up.

The judgment was short, because the magistrate still wanted to be home before dark. The girl was alive, and so no death would be recorded. The charter was hers by blood and by sign, and because she was a child it would be held in trust until she came of age. Her guardian would be the person who had kept her alive when her own household had not, and the only person on the bridge who fit that description was an old woman in a patched oilskin whom the town had once driven into the Reach. Osric would answer before the county court for declaring a living child dead in order to take what was hers. And the toll-house, which had never been Maren's to keep without the charter, would pass back to the ford.

Maren came forward then, for the first time. She stopped an arm's length from her daughter, and for a moment it looked as though she would kneel, or weep, or say the thing that mothers say in stories. Ailis waited, the way she had waited in the Reach. But whatever Maren had come to say, she could not find the beginning of it, and in the end she only said her daughter's name.

Ailis looked at her mother for a long time. You told me to keep it lit, she said. I did. Then she picked the brass lantern up off the table and turned away, toward Tamsin, toward the end of the bridge, and she did not look back. She did not need to. There was nothing her mother could say now that she still needed to hear.

They made the old watch-house above the ford into a home that winter. Tamsin swept out the swallows' nests and patched the roof, and Ailis hung the lantern in the window facing the river, and every night she lit it. Tamsin taught her to trim a wick so that it burned without smoke, to read the river by the colour of its foam, and to say no to grown men in a voice that did not shake. People in Carrow Ford began to walk a little differently past the watch-house. Some of them came to say they were sorry. Some brought the children they had once frightened with Tamsin's name, so the children could see that she was real, and kind, and had only ever been right.

And every night, when the lantern was lit, a great grey shape came gliding down the valley and settled on the cliff above the ford, where the old wardens had once kept their watch. She never made a sound. She did not need to. The crossing was kept by the marked, and the marked were kept by the grey, and the girl in the window, who had once been left alone in the dark, was never left alone in it again.
